exp.2:30:
It says that the Lord will not reject or abandon his people forever. "Cast off" means to reject or push something aside, and "for ever" indicates that this rejection will not be final. The pain may be real, but it has a limit.

The one speaking in Lamentations is a poet mourning the destruction of Jerusalem, probably at the time of the Babylonian conquest. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the book does not state this explicitly. In chapter 3, in the midst of his anguish, the author remembers who God is and holds on to hope. The verses that follow explain that, although God brings affliction, he also shows compassion.

Today, when you go through a painful season, do not interpret it as the end of your story with God. Tell him honestly what you feel, and remember his past mercies. His silence or his discipline are not eternal abandonment.
exp.3:12:
This verse explains why Jerusalem fell: the blame rests on its spiritual leaders. The prophets and priests, who were meant to guide the people in truth and justice, failed badly. The phrase "that have shed the blood of the just" means that they caused the death of innocent people, or allowed it to happen.

Lamentations is a song of mourning, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. The author grieves the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon. Here he recognizes that the disaster was no accident: corrupt leaders bore a heavy responsibility. The verses that follow show them wandering like blind people, stained with blood.

Those who teach or lead others carry a greater responsibility. Today we can pray for our pastors and leaders, and honestly examine how we use any influence we have, so that it is exercised with integrity and not with selfishness.
exp.1:0:
This verse is a lament. It says that God, in his anger, covered Jerusalem, called here the daughter of Zion, with darkness. The glory of Israel was thrown from heaven down to the earth, meaning it lost its honor and its height. The footstool of his feet is usually understood as the temple or the ark, the place where God was felt to be present.

Lamentations is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not name its author. The poet mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 586 BC. He interprets that ruin as the consequence of God's judgment for the people's sin, and he expresses it with grief and amazement.

For today: when we go through losses or painful consequences, we can weep honestly before God, without pretending. And even in the midst of pain, we can acknowledge our mistakes and return to him, trusting in his mercy.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that God destroyed without pity the homes and defenses of the people of Judah. The "dwellings of Jacob" are the people's homes; the "strongholds" are their walled cities. The word "polluted" means that he stripped the kingdom and its rulers of their honor and dignity.

Lamentations is a song of grief, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. The speaker mourns the fall of Jerusalem, which took place in 586 BC at the hands of Babylon. The poet sees it as God's judgment for the people's sin, and that is why he speaks with such raw honesty.

For today: we can be honest with God in our pain, without hiding what we feel. And when the consequences of our mistakes overtake us, this invites us to return to him with humility, remembering that later in the same book it speaks of his mercy that is renewed every morning.
exp.3:16:
They say the people grew tired of looking and waiting for help that never came. "Exhausted" means worn out, without strength. "Useless help" is a help that is of no use, that did nothing. They hoped a neighboring nation would save them, but those people had no power to do it.

The speaker is the people of Judah, who mourn the fall of Jerusalem. Many believe the book was written by Jeremiah, although the text does not say so directly. While the city was under siege, they sought human allies, probably Egypt, instead of turning back to God. The text shows the disappointment of someone who trusted in the wrong thing.

For today: think about what things you hope will rescue you, such as money, influence, or people. They can fail. Bring your burdens to God in prayer and trust in Him first, without despising the good help others may be able to give you.
exp.2:47:
He says the writer weeps without stopping, as though his eyes were rivers of water. The reason is the destruction of the daughter of his people, that is, the ruin and grief of his nation. "Daughter of my people" is a poetic way of speaking about the nation, with tenderness. The destruction here means ruin or a deep wound.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem, which was destroyed by the Babylonians. Its enemies mocked, and the people suffered. The verses that follow show that he waits until God looks down and sees from heaven.

Today we can weep with those who suffer, without offering hasty advice. And when the pain is great, we can bring those tears to God, trusting that He sees.
exp.2:52:
The explanation says that the speaker was shut away in a dark pit or dungeon, and that the opening was sealed with a stone. A "dungeon" is an underground prison, and "cut off my life" suggests they took away his life and his freedom. The stone over him gives the sense of being buried, with no way out.

Lamentations mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. The speaker expresses his grief in a personal way, and it is not clear whether he refers to his own experience, to that of Jeremiah (whom tradition links to the book), or to that of the whole people. His enemies hunted him without cause, like someone hunting a bird. That is why the next verse speaks of waters covering him and of calling on God from the depths.

When you feel shut in and without a way out, do not keep your pain silent. Cry out to God with sincerity, as this man did, because He hears even from the darkest place.
exp.1:3:
This verse describes God as a warrior who prepares to fight against his own people. The first quoted phrase, "Entesó su arco," means that he drew his bow taut, ready to shoot. The phrase about killing "all that was lovely in sight" refers to what was most dear and precious in Jerusalem. The phrase "the tent of the daughter of Zion" is a poetic way of speaking of the city and its homes. His anger fell like fire.

Lamentations is a song of mourning, and tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. The author mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, in the year 586 BC. He understands that ruin as the consequence of the people's sin, and so he speaks with pain and raw honesty.

For today: when we go through losses or discipline, we can weep sincerely before God, without disguising the pain. And since the book moves forward, we can also hope in his mercy.
exp.2:41:
It says the people acknowledge their guilt. "We have transgressed and have rebelled" means they rose up against God, and "we have not been faithful" means they failed him in their loyalty. Then it adds: "thou hast not pardoned," that is, at that moment they feel God has not taken away the punishment.

The speaker is the prophet, probably Jeremiah according to tradition, together with the people of Judah. They mourn the destruction of Jerusalem. First there is an invitation to examine one's own life and return to God, and here they confess their sin. What follows shows their pain, because they feel God is distant and angry.

For today: before we complain to God about our suffering, we can be honest and confess our faults. Acknowledging the wrong is not the end, but the first step toward returning to Him, who promises to forgive the one who repents.
exp.2:24:
The explanation says that God is good to those who trust in him and wait for him, that is, to the one who seeks him with all their heart. The word "Lord" here is the name of God as it appears in the verse. "Wait" here does not only mean enduring the passing of time, but trusting with patience. "Soul" refers to the whole person, with their desires and their inner life. "Seeketh" means "seeks."

Lamentations expresses grief over the destruction of Jerusalem, and tradition usually attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so openly. The speaker comes out of deep suffering, but in the middle of it recalls that God is faithful and that his mercies are renewed every morning. He says, "The Lord is my portion," and for that reason he decides to wait.

Today, when a hard situation drags on, you can begin the day praying simply: "Lord, you are my portion; today I seek you and trust in you." Waiting on God is not becoming passive, but moving forward with faith and patience.
exp.2:29:
The person who suffers, he says, will offer his cheek to the one who strikes him, and will be full of disgrace. That is, he will endure many insults and humiliations without answering with revenge.

Lamentations mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Here a man speaks who has suffered greatly (tradition links him to Jeremiah, though the book does not give his name). He accepts the punishment in silence and humility, waiting on God. The verses that follow explain why: the Lord does not reject forever, and his compassion is great.

For today: when you are offended or treated unjustly, try not to respond with anger right away. Keep silent, pray, and trust that God is compassionate and can sustain you. This does not mean accepting abuse, but waiting on God without returning evil for evil.
exp.3:20:
It says that Edom, which rejoiced to see Jerusalem fall, will not escape. "Daughter of Edom" refers to the people of Edom, a neighbor of Judah. "Uz" was a region linked to Edom, though its exact location is debated. The "cup" represents God's judgment, and "drunken" means that Edom will receive it until it staggers. "Naked" shows a shameful fall. The tone is ironic: "rejoice" is almost mocking.

The poet of Lamentations speaks on behalf of a people wounded by the fall of Jerusalem (around 586 B.C.). Tradition usually attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so. Edom had celebrated Judah's misfortune. The following verse promises that Zion's punishment will end and that Edom will answer for its sins.

Today: do not rejoice when someone falls, even if they have hurt you. Place your pain and your desire for justice in God's hands, and ask him for a compassionate heart.
exp.1:17:
The people, with broken hearts, cried out to God. Then the poet speaks to the wall of Jerusalem as if it were a person and asks it to weep without stopping, like a stream, day and night. "The apple of your eye" means the pupil, that is, the eye itself: do not let them stop weeping. The Hebrew text of the first sentence is difficult, and some translate it in a different way.

Lamentations was written after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. The author sees the people's pain, the mockery of their enemies, and the hunger of the children, and encourages the city to bring its sorrow to God.

Today we can speak with God honestly about what hurts us. Weeping before Him is not a lack of faith; it is trusting that He listens to us.
exp.4:1:
Our inheritance has passed to strangers, and our houses to outsiders. The explanation says that the land and the houses God had given Israel as an inheritance now belong to others. "Inheritance" is property that is received from one's parents, and "strangers" and "outsiders" are people from outside, who are not part of the people.

The words "turned to" in the verse would today be "passed to."

The speaker is the people of Judah, who pray to God after the fall of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so directly. The people suffer the loss of their land, their security and their dignity, and they ask God to remember and to look upon their shame.

For today: when you feel you have lost something important, such as a home, a job or stability, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. You can tell God honestly, as this people does. Sincere prayer is the first step toward finding comfort and hope.
exp.1:21:
He says that God called the terrors from every side, as people are called to a solemn feast. On the day of his anger no one escaped or was left alive. The children that the voice of the poem cared for and raised, the enemy destroyed. The word "á" is the same as "a," the word for young men is what the earlier wording used for them, and the word for "destroyed" in that line means that the enemy wiped them out.

The poet speaking in Lamentations is traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. He mourns Jerusalem, destroyed by Babylon in 586 B.C. He understands it as God's judgment for the people's sin, and so he uses the image of a feast: God himself "invited" the disaster. It is a lament full of pain, not a cold explanation.

For today: when the pain is very great, you can bring it to God honestly, without pretending. He allows his people to speak to him with tears, and he also hears the cry of the one who suffers.
exp.2:63:
The speaker asks God to give his enemies what they deserve, according to the wrong they have done. Here "give them the payment they deserve" is rendered simply as "repay them what is due," and "the work of their hands" refers to their actions. The name of God is the Lord.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He speaks in the middle of grief over the fall of Jerusalem. He feels persecuted, mocked all day long, turned into a song of ridicule. He did not take revenge himself; he brought his complaint to God and asked him for justice.

For today: when someone has hurt you, you can honestly tell God your pain and leave justice in his hands, instead of seeking revenge. Jesus also teaches us to pray for those who harm us (Matthew 5:44).
exp.0:11:
It says that Jerusalem, speaking like a wounded person, addresses everyone who passes by on the road. She asks them whether her suffering means nothing to them, and urges them to look closely: is there any pain like hers? She acknowledges that this pain comes from the Lord, who afflicted her on the day of his burning anger. The sentence about "means nothing to them" is explained as "it matters to you" or "it touches your heart." The word for "burning anger" is intense, fierce wrath.

The speaker is Jerusalem, pictured as a woman. The book mourns the destruction of the city, probably by the Babylonians, in 586 B.C. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so. The people have lost their wealth, have seen their temple invaded, and are going hungry. She understands that this is the consequence of her rebellion.

When you suffer, do not keep it in silence. Tell God your pain honestly, as this book does, and seek out people who will listen. And if you see someone suffering, do not walk past: stop and stand with them.
exp.1:2:
It says that God, in his anger, took away all the strength of Israel. The "horn" was a symbol of strength, like that of a bull. It also says that God withdrew his "right hand," that is, his hand of protection, when the enemy came. His anger burned against Jacob, that is, against the people, like a fire that consumes everything around it.

The author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly, speaks here. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem before Babylon, in the year 586 BC. He understands this ruin as the consequence of God's judgment for the people's sin, and he describes it with grief.

Today we can learn to be honest with God in our pain, without hiding our tears. This book teaches us to lament before Him, and to keep seeking Him even when everything seems lost, trusting that his mercy does not run out (Lamentations 3:22-23).
exp.1:13:
It says that the prophets of Jerusalem announced false and worthless things to the people. "Empty deceit and folly" are hollow lies with no sense in them. They did not show the people their sin so that they would repent and avoid exile, which is being carried off into a foreign land. Instead, they gave "empty prophecies and misleading messages," that is, deceptive messages that led the people off the right path.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns for Jerusalem after its destruction by Babylon. Before the disaster, many prophets said that everything would be fine, and for that reason no one responded in time.

For today: let us look for voices that tell the truth with love, even when it hurts, and not only words that comfort us. Let us ask God for humility to hear correction and return to Him in time.
exp.2:40:
This verse invites us to pray with our whole being. To lift up our hearts with our hands means that the gesture of raising our hands should be joined to a sincere heart. The phrase "to God in the heavens" is the same thought in its fuller form: it is not enough to make an outward gesture, because God looks at the inside.

The one speaking is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the text does not say so explicitly. Jerusalem has been destroyed and the people are suffering. Instead of complaining, the author calls for examining one's own life and returning to God. The verses that follow admit the people's rebellion and express grief over the judgment they have received.

For today: when you are in difficulty, before you complain, pause. Be honest with God, acknowledge what you need to correct, and pray with an open heart, trusting that He listens.
exp.4:6:
The explanation says that the people's ancestors sinned and are no longer here, yet now their children are the ones suffering the consequences. The phrase "they are not" in the verse means "they are gone," and the verse's words "and we have borne their iniquities" mean that the people carry the weight of their guilt.

The speakers are the people of Judah in Lamentations 5, a communal prayer after the fall of Jerusalem. They are humbled, poor, and ruled by others. They feel the pain of inheriting the results of earlier wrongs. Some scholars note that other biblical texts show each generation was also responsible for its own sin (Ezekiel 18). Here the people simply voice their complaint and their sorrow.

For today: we can be honest with God about the wounds we inherit, such as broken families or bad habits. We can also ask him to break that cycle in us, and begin, with his help, to choose a different path for those who come after us.
exp.2:9:
In the grief of the one speaking, God seems to him like a bear lying in wait, ready to attack, or like a lion hidden in dark places.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not state this clearly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. He speaks honestly from his suffering and feels that God is against him. This is his perception in the middle of pain, and the book later returns to hope in the faithfulness of God (3:21-26).

For today: when you feel that God is far away or is hard on you, you do not have to pretend. You can tell him honestly what you feel, as this writer does, and keep seeking him, trusting that his mercy does not run out.
exp.2:58:
The speaker asks God to look at the injustice he is suffering and to take up his defense. "Wrong" means an offense or unfair treatment. "Judge my cause" is like asking a lawyer to speak on your behalf in a court case. It is a prayer of trust: you have already seen it, Lord; now act.

The one speaking in Lamentations is a poet who grieves over the destruction of Jerusalem and the mockery of its enemies. He is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. In this passage he recalls that God had heard and rescued him before, and that is why he dares to ask for help again.

When someone treats you unjustly, you do not have to take revenge or prove that you are right at all costs. Tell God honestly what happened, remember how he helped you before, and leave your case in his hands.
exp.4:11:
The explanation says the enemies hanged the princes, that is, the leaders of the people. This may mean they were hanged by their hands, or that they were executed by order of the invaders; scholars understand it in several ways. Also, they did not honour the elders: the phrase about not honouring the faces of the old men means that they gave them no honour at all.

Here the people of Judah speak in prayer. Lamentations 5 is a cry after the fall of Jerusalem. The book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so. The people describe their humiliation: hunger, violence and the loss of their leaders, and they bring it before God.

For today: when the pain is so great that there are no words, we can speak to God with complete sincerity. And we should honour and care for the elderly, for God values them.
exp.3:18:
It says that the enemies of Jerusalem were swifter than the eagles. They pursued them over the mountains and laid traps for them in the wilderness. Ambushes are surprise attacks launched from a hiding place. The point is that there was nowhere to run and no safe place.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, around 586 B.C. The people had hoped for help from allies who could not save them, and not even the king managed to escape.

When everything seems lost, it is wise not to place our hope in human resources that fail. We can be honest with God about our pain, as this book is, and seek in Him a refuge that does not disappoint us.
exp.0:20:
Jerusalem cries out in pain, and no one comforts her. Her enemies heard of her misfortune and rejoiced, knowing that God allowed it. She asks God to bring the day he announced, so that they will suffer the same as she does. The word "they are glad" in the verse is the word for "rejoiced" that you see here.

Jerusalem speaks here, pictured as a widow left alone after Babylon destroyed the city. She acknowledges that her fall came because of her rebellion. Her plea for justice against her enemies is a cry of pain; many interpreters see in it the desire that God also judge those who were cruel to her.

When you feel alone and without comfort, do not hide your pain. Bring it to God honestly, even acknowledging your failures. He hears those who cry out, and you can leave justice in his hands rather than taking revenge.
exp.0:0:
It says that Jerusalem, who was once full of people and admired among the nations, is now alone and empty. The writer compares her to a widow: without a husband, without protection, and without support. "Populous" means full of inhabitants. "Tributary" means that she must now pay taxes or tribute to others, like a conquered people. She who once ruled over other regions is now dominated.

The book is a lament over the destruction of Jerusalem, probably when Babylon conquered her in 586 B.C. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, but the text does not name its author. The one speaking weeps with grief for his city and acknowledges that her fall was the consequence of the people's disobedience.

For today: God allows us to weep honestly. When you feel loss or loneliness, do not hide it; bring it to God in prayer, for He hears honest lament.
exp.2:7:
What it says: The speaker feels that God does not hear him. Although he cried out for help and raised his voice, he feels that God has shut out his prayer, as if unwilling to pay attention. Two of the source's quoted phrases and the note about an old spelling are not part of this verse, so they are left out here.

Context: Lamentations is a book of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. In this chapter, the speaker describes his pain with harsh images: darkness, chains, and blocked paths. He expresses how he feels, not necessarily the whole truth about God. Later in the same chapter, hope returns (3:21-26).

For today: If at some point you feel that God is keeping silent, do not hide your pain. You can tell him honestly, as this writer does. Praying without pretending is also faith. Keep crying out, and seek the support of other believers.
exp.1:19:
What it says: Jerusalem asks God to look at her suffering and to consider who has been made to suffer so much. She asks whether it is right that mothers should end up eating their own little children, and whether the priest and the prophet should be killed in the holy place. Where the verse speaks of the one who is in such pain, the word "behold" means "look closely," and the words "fruit" and "children" refer to the children.

Context: The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so clearly. He speaks after Jerusalem was destroyed by Babylon, around 586 BC. There was hunger and death, and the writer dares to bring his complaint before God with tears, hiding nothing.

For today: When pain overwhelms you, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God with complete honesty what you feel, even with hard questions. Honest prayer is also faith, because you keep coming to Him.
exp.2:12:
God, like an archer, took the arrows he kept in his quiver (the case where arrows are carried) and drove them deep into the body of the one speaking. The arrows stand for pain, and the "kidneys" stand for the innermost part of a person: their feelings and their inner self.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, who mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Many believe it is Jeremiah, though the book does not say so openly. In this chapter he expresses his grief with very strong images, feeling that God himself has struck him. It is the honest language of someone who is suffering, not a complete explanation of who God is; later in the same chapter, hope in his mercy appears.

Today, if you are hurt, you can speak to God with complete honesty, without pretending. He hears the lament, and an honest prayer can be the way toward hope.
exp.0:10:
It says that all the people of Jerusalem are sighing as they search for bread. To get food, they have given away their treasures and valuable things, only to keep their lives going, that is, to stay alive. In the end, the city asks God to look at it, because it feels crushed and humiliated.

Here Jerusalem speaks, personified as a woman who is suffering. After the invasion and the siege, there is hunger and poverty. The book understands this as a consequence of the people's sin, but it also lets us see real grief. According to tradition, Jeremiah wrote the book, although the text does not say so directly.

For today: when you are exhausted or in need, do not pretend to be strong. You can pray honestly, with a prayer like this: "See, Lord, how I am." God is not offended by your pain, and you can also ask for help from people you trust.
exp.3:19:
The explanation says that the king of Judah, who was like the breath of life for the people, was captured by their enemies. The breath of our nostrils is the king, chosen by God. The people believed that under his protection they would live safely, even among the nations. The pits were hunting traps, and he was caught means that he was trapped.

The one speaking is the people of Jerusalem, mourning the fall of the city before Babylon in 586 BC. Many understand that it refers to King Zedekiah, who was captured after fleeing. His fall left the people without human hope. The book shows grief, but it also recognizes that God was at work in the judgment.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in leaders, institutions, or people, however good they may be. All of them can fail. We can thank them and pray for them, but our firmest trust must rest in God, who never falls.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that God took away his "tabernacle" as if it were the booth of a garden, meaning something fragile that is easily taken apart. That "tabernacle" is the temple, the "place of his assembly." It also says that God caused the appointed feasts and the sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, and that in the heat of his anger he rejected the king and the priest. "Solemn feasts" are religious festivals. "Despised" means rejected.

The speaker is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the text does not say so. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC). He understands that ruin as the consequence of God's judgment on the people's disobedience.

Today, this text reminds us that no building or religious routine can replace a sincere relationship with God. We can draw near to Him with humility, and weep honestly when there is pain, trusting in his mercy.
exp.0:7:
Jerusalem sinned greatly, and for this reason she was "removed," that is, taken from her place and her dignity. Those who used to honor her now despise her, because they have seen her "shame," which here means her nakedness or public humiliation. She sighs, groans with pain, and "turns backward," which can be understood as drawing back in shame or turning her face away.

The book mourns the fall of Jerusalem to the Babylonians, around 586 B.C. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not state this clearly. Here the poet speaks, describing the city as a wounded woman and acknowledging that her suffering is tied to her sin and rebellion.

For today: when we fail, it is not good to hide our shame or blame others. We can acknowledge the truth with humility and cry out to God, for the same book later reminds us that his mercies never end.
exp.0:13:
Jerusalem describes her own sins as a yoke, a heavy wooden frame fastened around the neck of an animal. Those rebellions are twisted together and now press down on her neck, the back of her neck. Her strength has failed. The Lord has handed her over to enemies she can no longer withstand.

The one speaking is the city of Jerusalem, portrayed as a suffering woman. Lamentations is a song of mourning over the fall of the city, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so explicitly. The poem acknowledges that this ruin is connected to the people's rebellion, so the grief is mixed with confession.

For today: when you carry the consequences of your own mistakes, do not hide them or sink into despair. Acknowledge them honestly before God, asking for his forgiveness and his help to get back on your feet.
exp.2:20:
The writer decides to bring to mind, or to "set again in his heart," one specific thought, and that is why he can keep on hoping.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem and the suffering of his people. Just before this, he sinks into his grief, but here he changes direction. What he recalls comes in the following verses: the mercy and faithfulness of God, which never come to an end.

When pain overwhelms you, do not ignore what you feel, but also choose to remember who God is. You can write down three times when He helped you and go over them when distress comes. In this way your hope rests on His character, not on your circumstances.
exp.2:1:
It says that God led him and brought him along a path of darkness, not of light. The words "guided me" and "brought me" are older forms of "led me" and "brought me." The "darkness" is the dark, and here it stands for pain, confusion, and having no sense of direction.

The one speaking is a man who suffers greatly, and so he says: "I am the one who has seen affliction." The book of Lamentations mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the text does not name him. Some think this "man" represents the whole people. He feels that God's punishment weighs on him, and he speaks with sincerity and pain.

For today: when you pass through a dark season, you do not have to pretend that everything is fine. You can tell God honestly what you feel. This chapter does not end in darkness; later it speaks of the faithfulness of God (3:22-23).
exp.4:5:
It says the people "gave the hand" to Egypt and to Assyria, that is, they submitted to them or made alliances with them, in order to get bread. "Being satisfied with bread" means having enough food. In other words, they sought help from powerful nations so that they would not go hungry.

The book of Lamentations is a lament over the fall of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so directly. Here the people speak, confessing their misery and their dependence on foreign powers. Some think Egypt and Assyria represent political alliances of the past; others, that they are symbolic names for any power that dominated them. There is no single interpretation that can be held with certainty.

For today: when we are in need, it is easy to trust anything that promises security. We can work and seek help wisely, but we should ask ourselves where our heart truly rests. God remains the one who sustains us.
exp.2:45:
All their enemies have spoken against them with scorn and attacked them with their words. "Opening the mouth" against someone can mean mocking them, speaking with contempt, or shouting with joy over their downfall. Here it is understood mainly as mockery and accusation.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not give his name.
