He says that God filled him with bitter things until he was satisfied. The words for being filled and made drunk in the verse refer to being filled completely and being made to drink until dizzy. Wormwood is a plant with a very bitter taste, a symbol of suffering and deep sorrow. It is an image of pain that leaves no room for anything else.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem and expresses his pain in the first person, perhaps as the voice of the whole people. He attributes his suffering to the hand of God, and speaks with raw honesty, without softening what he feels.

For today: you do not have to pretend that everything is fine before God. You can tell him sincerely how much something hurts you. Lamentations shows that honest complaint is also prayer, and later in this same chapter, hope returns.
exp.2:37:
It says that everything that happens is under the authority of God, the Most High. It asks whether both calamity and good do not come out of his mouth. The word "evil" here refers to calamities or misfortunes, not to moral wickedness. The verse before it asks who can say that something happened without the Lord permitting or commanding it.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. In the midst of the pain, he acknowledges that God governs even the suffering of the people. Then he invites us to examine our own lives and return to the LORD, without complaining against Him.

For today: when a difficulty comes, instead of complaining bitterly, stop and pray. Ask God to show you whether there is something to correct, and trust that He is still good and still hears you.
exp.2:8:
He has blocked the path of the one speaking with walls of cut and shaped stone, that is, large, firm stones that cannot be moved. He has also twisted his paths: he made them confusing and full of turns, so that he could not move forward with clarity.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He speaks in the midst of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. He feels enclosed, with no way out and no answer from God. It is language of complaint and suffering, expressed with strong images. Later in this same chapter, the tone shifts toward hope in God's mercy.

If today you feel that everything is closed off and you cannot see a way out, you can tell God so honestly, as this text does. Praying in pain is not a lack of faith. And keep reading: hope comes afterward.
exp.3:11:
It says that no one in the world, neither the kings nor ordinary people, thought that an enemy could enter through the gates of Jerusalem. It seemed like a safe city. The enemy and the one who opposes them are the same idea here, and "all the inhabitants of the world" refers to all the peoples that were known.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations. A tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. The verses that follow explain that it happened because of the sin of the people's leaders, and that made the surprise even more painful.

For today: let us not trust that something is secure just because it has always been that way. Our true security lies in living with humility and faithfulness before God, and in listening to his correction in time.
exp.1:14:
The explanation says that the people passing by Jerusalem mocked her. "Clap their hands" was clapping or striking the palms as a sign of scorn, and "hiss" and wagging the head expressed contempt. They asked, "Is this the city that men call the perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth?"

The one speaking is the poet of Lamentations, who mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. Many think it was Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. The text explains that the fall came because of the sin of the people and because of prophets who gave false hope instead of warning. The neighbors, far from offering comfort, mocked.

For today: when you see someone fall, do not mock or rejoice. Offer them compassion and, if needed, an honest word spoken in love.
exp.0:18:
It says that Jerusalem called for help from her "lovers," that is, the allies she trusted, but they betrayed her. It also says that her priests and elders, the leaders of the people, died inside the city while they were searching for food to keep themselves alive. To keep her life going a little longer means to keep it sustained for a while longer.

The speaker is the city of Jerusalem, personified as a weeping woman, after the destruction by Babylon. She acknowledges that the LORD is righteous and that she rebelled against him. Many understand the "lovers" as allied nations or false gods; the text does not make this entirely clear. The hunger of the siege left everyone weakened, even the leaders.

For today: when human securities fail us, we can stop seeking support in what does not sustain us and turn back to God with sincerity, acknowledging our faults and asking him for comfort.
exp.1:7:
It says that God himself decided to tear down the walls of Jerusalem, called "the daughter of Zion." The phrase "stretched out the line" referred to measuring with a cord, as builders do, but here it describes demolishing with precision. The outer wall in front of the main wall is the low barrier before the principal wall. Both walls mourn and fall together, as if the city itself were weeping.

Lamentations is a funeral song for the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, in 586 B.C. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. The poet sees the destruction as the result of God's judgment on the people's persistent sin, and he expresses it with pain, not with coldness.

For today: when we go through losses, we can bring our pain to God honestly, without pretending. Lamenting is also a form of faith, because we keep speaking with Him, and the book later speaks of his mercy that is renewed every morning.
exp.3:5:
It says that the wickedness of Jerusalem ("the daughter of my people") was greater than the sin of Sodom. Sodom was destroyed in a moment, all at once, and no hands were laid on her to besiege her. Jerusalem, by contrast, suffered a long and painful punishment. "Iniquity" means wickedness. "Was overthrown" means that she was destroyed.

The author of Lamentations, traditionally Jeremiah, though the book does not say so, speaks here. He mourns for Jerusalem after she was besieged and destroyed by Babylon. The verses around it describe the terrible hunger: children without bread and the wealthy reduced to misery. The poet recognizes that this suffering is tied to the sin of the people.

For today: we can learn to see the consequences of sin with humility, without excuses. If there is something God points out to you, do not wait for the pain to grow; return to Him soon, for his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.0:15:
He says the one speaking weeps without stopping. His eyes run with water, meaning the tears flow like a river. He weeps because the comforter has gone far from him, someone who would bring rest or relief to his soul. His children are ruined and lost because the enemy has won and overcome them.

The one speaking is Jerusalem, pictured as a suffering woman, though the book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah (the tradition says so, but the text does not give his name). After the city fell to Babylon, the people are in ruins and in captivity. She acknowledges that her own rebellions had a part in this pain.

For today: when you are hurt, do not hide your weeping. Bring it honestly to God and also seek out people who can walk with you. Crying is not a lack of faith; it is an honest way to ask for comfort.
exp.0:19:
Here Jerusalem asks God to look at her distress. She says her bowels are troubled, meaning she feels a deep pain, like a knot in the stomach, and that her heart is turned within her, stirred up inside. She acknowledges that she has grievously rebelled. Abroad the sword bereaves, which means the sword leaves mothers without children. And at home there is as death: hunger, sickness, and mourning.

The city of Jerusalem speaks, personified as a grieving woman, after being destroyed and after her people were taken into exile. Many understand that the book was written by Jeremiah, though the text does not say so directly. She recognizes that God is righteous and that her suffering is tied to her sin.

For today: when you suffer or have failed, do not hide from God. Bring Him your pain and your guilt with sincerity, trusting that He listens.
exp.2:27:
The explanation says that the person who suffers will sit alone and keep silent, because God allowed him to bear that burden, a heavy weight. The word "sitteth" in the verse means "sits", and the phrase "hath borne it upon him" means he has laid it upon his shoulders.

The one speaking in this chapter is a man who suffers deeply after the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not state this directly. He describes his pain, but in the midst of it he remembers that God is faithful and that it is worth waiting on Him with humility.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not rush to complain to everyone. Find a quiet moment alone, still your anxiety, and pray calmly, waiting on God. Silence is not giving up, but trusting that He is at work even when we cannot see it.
exp.3:17:
They tracked our every step, so that we could not walk freely in our streets. The enemies watched the people of Jerusalem like hunters following their prey, and the residents could no longer move about their own city in safety. "They hunt our steps" means that they spied on them and lay in wait for them. "Our end is near" speaks of the end of the city, and "our days are fulfilled" means that their time had run out.

The poet of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly, mourns with his people the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. The verses nearby mention a hope placed in allies who could not save them, and the text sees this as a consequence of the people's sin.

For today: when everything falls apart, it is wise to stop trusting human supports that fail. We can be honest with God in our pain, as this poet is, and place our hope in Him again.
exp.1:12:
Here the writer speaks directly to Jerusalem, whom he calls "daughter" and "virgin." He asks what example or comparison he could use to comfort her. He finds none, because her wound is "great like the sea," that is, vast and impossible to measure. He ends by asking who can heal her. "Breach" means ruin or destruction.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, whom tradition attributes to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so openly. He mourns for Jerusalem after its fall to Babylon. He has just described the hunger of the children in the streets. The verses that follow point out that the false prophets did not warn the people about their sin.

Today, when someone suffers a very great pain, there is no need to offer quick explanations. Accompanying them with tenderness and prayer means a great deal. And let us remember that only God can heal the deepest wounds.
exp.2:43:
He says that God wrapped himself in a cloud, like a thick curtain, so that the prayer of the people would not reach him. The phrase "that our prayer should not pass through" is an image: the people feel that God has closed the way and is not listening to them.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations (tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so). He speaks on behalf of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. He acknowledges his rebellion, but he also expresses his pain and his sense of being abandoned. It is the honest complaint of someone who suffers the consequences of his sin.

There are times when God seems silent and prayer feels empty. This verse shows that we can express that feeling with sincerity. Even so, the book moves on and arrives at hope: "his mercies are new every morning" (3:23). Keep praying, even when you feel no answer.
exp.2:57:
He says God took the place of a lawyer on behalf of the one who suffers. Where the verse reads "thou hast pleaded," it means you argued his case and defended him; "the causes of my soul" means my case, my deepest need. "Thou hast redeemed my life" means you rescued my life from death or danger, like someone who pays to set another person free.

The author of Lamentations speaks here, perhaps Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. After the fall of Jerusalem, he speaks of his grief and of his enemies. Here he looks back and remembers that God heard him when he cried out and said to him, "Fear not." That memory gives him encouragement to keep asking for help.

When you are distressed, remember the times God has sustained you. That memory can give you courage to pray again and to trust that He defends your cause.
exp.2:4:
He built a barrier against me, as one who builds a wall or fence around someone. He surrounded me with bitterness and sorrow. He also surrounded me with hardship, meaning weariness, grief, and suffering.

The one speaking is a poet who mourns the destruction of Jerusalem and the pain of his people. Tradition usually attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. In this chapter, the man describes his anguish as if God himself had turned against him. It is the language of sincere pain, not a complete explanation of who God is.

For today: when you feel that life is closing in on you with bitterness and exhaustion, you do not have to hide it. The Bible allows you to weep honestly before God. Tell him frankly what you feel; this same chapter, further on, reminds us that his mercies do not come to an end.
exp.2:26:
It is good for a person to learn to carry the yoke from a young age. The "yoke" was the wooden piece placed on animals for work; here it represents the burden, the discipline, or the suffering.

Lamentations reflects the grief over the destruction of Jerusalem (587 B.C.). Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the text does not state this clearly. The speaker here, in the midst of his anguish, remembers that God is good and faithful. Many understand the yoke as the trials God allows; others, as discipline in general. The verses that follow speak of waiting in silence and with humility.

For today: do not flee from every difficulty, and do not grow bitter because of it. The trials of youth, such as effort, patience, and obedience, can form a steady character and a faith that trusts in God. When something weighs on you, pray and wait on Him.
exp.3:21:
It says that the punishment of Jerusalem (the daughter of Zion) has now come to an end, and that God will not allow her to be carried away into exile again. Edom, however, will be visited: God will deal with its wickedness and expose its sins. To carry away means to take someone captive to another country; iniquity is wickedness or guilt.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. Edom, a neighboring nation, had rejoiced in that disaster. The poem ends with hope: Judah's suffering has a limit, and God also judges those who mock the pain of others. Some understand the "no more" to refer to that particular exile.

For today: when you go through a trial, trust that God sets a limit to suffering and does not forget his own. And avoid rejoicing at the fall of others; leave justice in God's hands.
exp.4:19:
It says that the people ask God in pain: "Why does it seem that you have forgotten us and left us alone for so long?" The phrase "for so long" refers to a very extended period. It is not that God really forgets, but that this is how his absence is felt.

Lamentations is a song of sorrow. The people of Judah speak after the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, probably by the Babylonians. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. Just before this, the people remember that God reigns forever, and that is why they dare to ask and to plead for restoration.

For today: when you feel forgotten by God, do not keep your pain silent. You can honestly bring him your questions, while also remembering that he remains faithful. Sincere prayer, even with tears, is a form of trust.
exp.3:8:
It says that it was better to die in war, by the sword, than to die of hunger. Whoever dies by the sword is soon finished; whoever dies of hunger wastes away "little by little," because the land no longer gave food. "By the sword" means "by the sword," and "fruits of the field" are the harvests and the food.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so clearly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to the Babylonians, around 586 B.C. The verses before describe how hunger disfigured even the healthiest and most distinguished people. The poet sees this suffering as part of God's judgment on the people's sin.

For today: do not minimize the long, quiet suffering of others. There are slow pains, such as poverty or illness, that need our constant compassion. And you can bring your laments to God with sincerity, as this book does.
exp.2:6:
It says that God, from the viewpoint of the one who suffers, has surrounded him on every side as in a prison, so that he cannot escape. The word "hedged" in the verse means "fenced in" or "closed around," and "chain" refers to the iron chains or shackles that were placed on the feet of prisoners. The phrase "made my chain heavy" means that he made his chains heavier.

The one speaking is a man who lives through the grief of the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition usually attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so clearly. Here he speaks in the language of complaint, like someone who feels God is against him. It is the feeling of the one who suffers, not a complete explanation of who God is. The same chapter later speaks of hope in the mercy of the Lord.

For today: if you feel trapped and without a way out, you can tell God honestly what you feel, even the rawest things. The Bible makes room for that honesty, and from there one can go on waiting on Him.
exp.2:34:
He says that God sees and does not overlook it when someone takes away from a person their right, that is, what is justly due to them. Turning aside a man's right means bending justice. Before the face of the Most High means that this happens in plain view of God, who is the supreme God. The verse is part of a list of injustices that the Lord does not approve.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, a poet who mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. In the middle of his grief, he remembers that God governs and that he is not indifferent to abuse, unjust imprisonment, or twisted justice. There are different ways of understanding the passage, but the comfort is that God is watching.

For today: if you have been treated unjustly, or if you have power over others, remember that God sees. Bring your pain to him in prayer, and deal justly with those who depend on you.
exp.2:13:
It says that the one speaking became a mockery to all his people. "Derision" means mockery or scorn. Also, he became the subject of their taunting songs, that is, the theme of their mocking chants, and this went on every day, without rest.

The speaker in Lamentations is a poet who suffers while Jerusalem lies in ruins, probably after the Babylonian invasion. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. In this passage, he feels that God himself has wounded him, like an archer aiming an arrow. To that pain is added the shame before his own people.

For today: if you are in pain and the mockery of others weighs on you, you can be honest with God, as this poet is. The Bible allows us to weep and complain in prayer. And later in this same chapter, hope returns as he remembers the faithfulness of God.
exp.2:25:
It is good to wait quietly and patiently for God's salvation. "Salvation" here does not refer to bodily health, but to the rescue or deliverance that comes from the Lord. Waiting in this way means not complaining or giving up in despair, but waiting with patience and trust.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah, although the book does not state this directly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem, in the midst of very great grief. Yet at this point he remembers that God is his portion and that He is good to those who seek Him. His hope comes from trusting the character of God, not from things looking better.

For today: when you are in a trial and see no way out, before reacting with anger or anxiety, pause for a few minutes in silence and pray. Remember that God is good, and trust that He is working even while you wait.
exp.1:6:
God himself, the explanation says, rejected his altar and despised his sanctuary, that is, the temple of Jerusalem. He allowed the enemy to seize the walls of the palaces. "They made a noise" means that the enemies shouted in the temple, just as the people used to shout with joy on the feast days. What once was a song of worship is now the shouting of enemy victory.

The book of Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem, in the year 586 B.C. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. The poet understands the fall as the consequence of God's judgment for the people's sin, and for that reason he speaks of God as "enemy."

For today: when the sacred becomes routine or mere appearance, God is not content with ceremonies. We can ask him for a sincere heart, and remember that, even in pain, the poet still addresses God.
exp.2:10:
It says that God, seen as a hunter or an enemy, made the author's path turn aside, tore him to pieces, and left him in ruin. The phrase for "turned aside" means the path was bent off its course. The phrase for "tore me to pieces" means he was broken apart. The phrase for "left me desolate" means he was left forsaken, destroyed, and alone. It is very strong and painful language.

The speaker is a man grieving over the fall of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so directly. He feels that God has treated him the way a wild animal treats its prey. This is the honest complaint of someone in suffering, not a complete explanation of God. Later in this same chapter, the author recalls the faithfulness of the Lord.

When pain leaves you without strength, you can tell God honestly what you feel, without disguising it. The Bible makes room for complaint. And then, like the author, try to remember God's mercy, which remains there even when you cannot feel it.
exp.2:16:
It says the suffering was so strong that the person felt peace had gone far away from their life. "Removed my soul far off from peace" means they lost their calm and their quiet. "I forgat prosperity" means they no longer remembered what was good, and could not feel that anything good existed.

The one speaking in this chapter is a man describing his grief after the destruction of Jerusalem. The book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. He speaks of bitterness and ruin, and in the verses that follow he admits that he nearly lost hope in God. But then he recalls the faithfulness of the Lord (v. 21-23).

When pain makes us forget what is good, we are not alone, and we are not poor believers for feeling it. We can do as he did: tell God honestly how we feel, and then calmly remember some of his past kindnesses, even if it is just one.
exp.0:16:
Zion, that is, Jerusalem, spreads out her hands asking for help, but no one comforts her. Spreading out the hands is a gesture of pleading or pain. According to the text, the Lord commanded that her enemies surround Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. Jerusalem became something repugnant to them, a thing despised and loathed.

Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem (587 B.C.). Here the city speaks as a personified figure, while the author, whom tradition often identifies with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so, describes her grief. The verse acknowledges that this disaster was not chance, but a consequence of God's judgment, as the following verse confirms: "the Lord is righteous."

Today, when you feel lonely or suffer the consequences of your mistakes, you can be honest before God, acknowledge your failure, and cry out to Him. He is the one who truly comforts.
exp.2:22:
The explanation says that God's mercies, mentioned in the previous verse, are renewed every day, like a fresh gift at dawn. And it recognizes that God's faithfulness is great, meaning that he keeps his word and does not abandon his people. "They are new every morning" means "they are renewed every day"; "mercies" means his kindness and compassion.

The speaker is the author of the book, traditionally identified as Jeremiah, although the text itself does not give his name. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem, in the midst of great sorrow. Right in the middle of the weeping, he decides to remember who God is, and that brings back his hope. That is why he says: "I will wait."

For today: at the start of the day, before thinking about your problems, take a moment to thank God for one concrete sign of his care. Even if yesterday was hard, today you have his new mercy, enough for whatever you face.
exp.4:20:
What it says: The people ask God: "Make us return to you, and then we will return." The word "turned" means "brought back." They also ask that God "renew" their days, that is, that He give them a new life, as in the good times at the beginning, when they were close to Him.

Context: The people of Judah speak in Lamentations, after the destruction of Jerusalem. They are suffering and feel abandoned. First they remember that God reigns forever, and then they ask why He seems to have forgotten them. The following verse shows their fear: perhaps God has rejected them completely. Some readers see this ending as a prayer full of hope; others see a painful and uncertain conclusion.

For today: When you feel far from God or tired of your failures, do not wait until you have strength of your own. Pray sincerely: "Lord, bring me back." He can give you the desire to return and renew your life.
exp.2:56:
The explanation says that on the same day the author called upon God, God drew near to him and answered: "Fear not." The word "drewest," in the verse you read, is the old form of "drew near," so the explanation's remark about the older form is not needed here. "I called upon" means "I called out" or "I asked for help." God did not stay far away; he made himself present and gave calm.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so explicitly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem. In this passage he speaks from a deep pit, which can be understood either as a real prison or as an image of extreme distress. He remembers that God had already heard him before, and so he dares to keep crying out.

For today: when you feel fear, speak with God honestly, even with only a few words. Then remember other times when he sustained you, and let his "Fear not" calm your heart.
exp.1:18:
It says that someone should rise up in the dead of night and cry out to God with complete sincerity. Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord would have been the picture of telling God everything we feel without holding anything back. Lifting up the hands was a gesture of prayer and pleading. Help is asked above all for the children, who faint from hunger at the corners of the streets.

Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the fall of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not state this clearly. The speaker describes the pain of the destroyed city and encourages Jerusalem not to stay silent, but to bring its anguish to God, even in the middle of judgment.

When sorrow overwhelms us, we do not have to pretend to be strong. We can pray honestly, weep before God, and intercede for those who suffer most near us, such as children and the vulnerable.
exp.2:15:
It says that God, seen by the one who suffers as the one who strikes him, made him eat bread with bits of gravel, and his teeth were broken. The word "gravel" in the verse refers to small stones or coarse grit. He also covered him with ashes, a sign of mourning, sorrow, and humiliation.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah. He weeps over the fall of Jerusalem and over his own pain. He speaks in very strong language, as he feels it in the middle of his suffering. But the book does not end here: shortly afterward it remembers that God's mercies do not come to an end.

For today: when pain leaves you without strength, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. Tell God honestly what you feel, as this passage does. And do not stop at the verse of discouragement; keep reading until you come to where hope returns.
exp.2:11:
He has drawn his bow, meaning he has readied it to shoot, and he has set me up as the target that the arrow is aimed at. The image is harsh: the writer feels that God has made him the mark of his attack.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so explicitly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem. In this passage he speaks of his pain in very strong language, the way he feels it. Later in the same chapter, hope returns as he remembers the mercy of God.

Today, if you are going through suffering that makes you feel abandoned, you can tell God honestly what you feel, hiding nothing. The Bible allows sincere lament, and sometimes hope comes after we pour out our hearts in prayer.
exp.2:44:
The explanation says that God made his people "offscouring and refuse" among the nations. "Offscouring" is what is scraped off and thrown away, like trash or waste. "Abomination" is something that causes disgust or rejection. "You made us" means "you made us into." It is a very harsh image: they feel despised by everyone.

The speaker of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so explicitly, mourns on behalf of the people after the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon (587-586 B.C.). He interprets the suffering as the consequence of God's judgment, and he feels that his prayers do not reach God.

Today, when you feel despised or cast aside, you can bring your pain to God with complete honesty, without pretending. This book shows that lamenting is also a form of faith, since it keeps speaking with God.
exp.0:12:
It says that God sent fire from above into the depths of the person, and that this pain overpowered her. He also spread a net to catch her feet and turned her back. The phrase that the fire took control means that the fire gained mastery over her. "Desolate" means destroyed and left empty. In the end, she is left with a pain that seems never to end.

The speaker is Jerusalem, pictured as a woman weeping after the fall of the city, probably before the Babylonians. The book is usually attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. She understands her suffering as the consequence of God's judgment for her rebellions, as the next verse shows. These are poetic images, not a literal description.

For today: when pain overwhelms us, we can speak about it with God honestly, without pretending to be strong. Lamentations teaches us that weeping before Him is also a form of faith.
exp.1:15:
This verse describes the enemies of Jerusalem mocking her after her fall. They open their mouths with contempt, hiss, and grind their teeth in rage. They say, "We have swallowed her up," and they celebrate that at last the day they had been waiting for has come.

The book of Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. The speaker describes the city's grief. Her enemies see her ruin as a victory, and the context says that God allowed this fall because of the people's sin.

For today: when someone falls or suffers, we should not rejoice in their pain. Instead, we should pray for that person, and if we ourselves are going through mockery or loss, we can bring our sorrow honestly before God.
exp.3:3:
This verse describes the suffering of infants during the famine. The nursing baby has its tongue stuck to the roof of its mouth from thirst, because it no longer receives milk. Young children ask for bread, but no one gives it out to them. The word "breaketh" in the verse refers to breaking bread into pieces and sharing it with each one, and here there is no one to do it.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so explicitly. He mourns for Jerusalem after the siege and the fall of the city. He compares mothers to ostriches, which were described as careless with their young, to show that the hunger was so severe that normal care had broken down. The poet understands this suffering as a consequence of the people's sin.

Today we can think of the smallest and most vulnerable people around us. God grieves for them. We can pray and, in concrete ways, share our bread with a family in need.
exp.4:21:
The explanation says that the people feel that God has rejected them completely and is very angry with them. The phrase "thou hast utterly rejected us" means "you have cast us far away without wanting to know anything about us." The word "wroth" means angry. Some read the verse as a question or a doubt: "Have you rejected us completely?" The Hebrew can be translated in more than one way.

The people speaking are the people of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem, probably in exile or among the ruins. Lamentations ends with a painful prayer. Just before it they ask: "Turn us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned." They acknowledge that they are suffering, but they do not stop crying out to God. The book does not end with a clear answer, but with an open plea.

When you feel far from God or hurt, do not keep silent. You can tell him honestly what you feel, even your doubts, and ask him to draw you close to himself. Honest prayer is also faith.
exp.3:0:
The explanation says that the gold, which was very valuable and bright, lost its shine and changed its appearance. The stones of the sanctuary, that is, of the temple, lie scattered at the corners and crossings of every street. What was beautiful and sacred has been destroyed and abandoned.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the fall of Jerusalem, which was destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BC. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not state this explicitly. The speaker weeps over the ruin of the city. The gold may represent the temple or the people themselves, and the following verses speak of the sons of Zion, once treasured like gold.

For today: God invites us to be honest about our pain. If something you valued has collapsed, you can weep before Him without pretending. The Bible makes room for that lament.
exp.4:8:
The explanation says that the people had to risk their lives just to get food. "We gat our bread" means that they went out to search for or gather food. "The sword of the wilderness" is a poetic way of speaking of the sword: the dangers from outside, such as armed gangs or thieves. Some think it may also refer to the heat and threat of the desert; the text allows both ideas.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the fall of Jerusalem. The speaker is the people of Judah, who describe their suffering after the destruction. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. With sorrow, they acknowledge the consequences of sin and the loss of security under the rule of strangers.

For today: if you know someone who works in fear or need to support their family, do not walk past. Pray for that person and help them in a concrete way, with food, work, or companionship.
exp.4:16:
It says the people are deeply sad. "Our heart has grown heavy" speaks of inner grief. "Our eyes have grown dim" means the eyes have darkened: their light has gone out, as when someone weeps so much or loses the hope that they no longer see clearly. "For this" points to everything before it: the lost joy, the mourning, and the fallen crown.

The speaker is the people of Judah, who after the destruction of Jerusalem acknowledge their sin and their suffering. The book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so explicitly. What saddens them is seeing Zion desolate, the place of God's presence. But the book ends by recalling that God reigns forever.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can bring your honest sadness to God, acknowledge what you did wrong if needed, and remember that He remains on His throne even when your eyes are dim.
exp.1:9:
The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground and say nothing. They throw dust on their heads and dress in sackcloth, a rough cloth used to show deep sorrow. The young women, who once had joy, bow their heads to the ground. "Daughter of Zion" is a poetic way of naming the city and its people.

The one speaking is the author of the book, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. He looks at the ruin of Jerusalem, probably the fall of 586 BC, and understands it as God's judgment for the people's sin. He describes the grief of everyone, from the elders to the young women.

For today: when the pain is so great that you have no words, you can be silent and weep before God. He does not ask you to pretend to be strong, but to come near to him with honesty.
exp.2:49:
The speaker says he will keep weeping "till" God looks down and sees from heaven. That is, his weeping will not stop until the Lord notices his pain and acts. "Look down and behold" expresses that God pays attention and intervenes, not merely that he observes.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, whom tradition identifies with Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. He weeps over the destruction of Jerusalem and the suffering of his people. His tears do not stop because he finds no relief, and he waits for God to respond.

Today we can bring our pain to God honestly, without hiding it. Weeping before Him is not a lack of faith; it is waiting for Him to see us. You can pray sincerely and trust that He hears, even when the answer takes time.
exp.3:10:
God says he let his full anger fall on Jerusalem, and he compares it to a fire that was kindled in Zion and burned down to its very base. The explanation of the word "accomplished" is that he carried his anger through to the end. The image of anger "poured out" is of wrath falling like hot liquid. The "foundations" are the base of the city.

Lamentations is a song of grief, and tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the book does not state this directly. The author mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians, around 586 BC. The verses that follow explain that it happened because of the sins of the people, of their prophets, and of their priests.

For today: God takes sin seriously, and we should hear this with humility. But this same book also speaks of his mercy, which is renewed every morning (3:22-23). We can return to him with sincerity and hope.
exp.0:8:
It says that Jerusalem has the filth of her sin stuck to her skirts, like a stain that cannot be hidden. "Her last end" means her final outcome or her future, and she did not think about what would come. That is why her fall was astonishing, and no one is there to comfort her. At the end, someone cries out to God: "O Lord, behold my affliction," because the enemy has made himself great.

This is the book of Lamentations, a song of grief after the destruction of Jerusalem. The poet speaks first, describing the city as a humbled woman, and in this part the city itself prays. The text links her fall with her sin, though not every detail of that time is told here.

For today: let us not ignore the consequences of our decisions, but let us also not stop praying. When you are wounded, even by your own mistakes, you can say honestly to God: "O Lord, behold my affliction."
exp.0:14:
He says that the Lord trampled all the brave men of Jerusalem who were within her. He also called together a force, an army, to destroy the young men. To trample is to tread down, and the young men are the youths. Judah, called the virgin daughter, was trodden down by the Lord the way grapes are trodden in the winepress, where the juice is squeezed out.

The one speaking is the city of Jerusalem, pictured as a suffering woman. Lamentations mourns the fall of the city, which many connect with the Babylonian conquest of 586 B.C. The poem acknowledges that this came because of the people's rebellions, and it describes it with very harsh images.

For today: we can bring our pain to God honestly, without covering it up. This book teaches us to lament and to recognize our failings, without losing hope that God remains our refuge.
exp.3:7:
It says that hunger changed people who were once admired so much that their face is darker than soot, and no one recognizes them in the street. Their skin clings to their bones, dried out and hard like a stick.

The word "visage" means their appearance or look, as the verse itself shows.

The author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly, speaks here. He weeps for Jerusalem after it was besieged and destroyed. The people described as having once been set apart and of noble appearance in the previous verse are now unrecognizable because of the siege. The poet shows the pain and the consequences of the people's sin.

Today we can look with compassion on those who suffer hunger or poverty, without judging them by their appearance. God draws near to the one who weeps, and we can help with something concrete: sharing food or supporting someone who needs it.
exp.0:5:
The explanation says that Jerusalem, called "daughter of Zion", lost all her splendor. "Beauty" refers to her glory, her peace and her dignity. Her leaders, that is, her rulers, became like weak deer that find no pasture. Without strength, they fled before the one who pursued them, that is, before the enemy who hounded them.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the fall of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book itself does not give his name. Here the poet speaks, mourning the ruined city. The text explains this ruin as the consequence of the people's rebellions against God, but it does so with deep sorrow, not with coldness.

For today: when life falls apart, we can bring our pain to God with honesty. Acknowledging our mistakes and grieving without pretending to be strong is a step toward hope.
exp.2:38:
This verse asks a question worth pondering: why should a person complain while still alive, when they are suffering the consequences of their own sin? The word for complaining here means to grumble with resentment, and the question points us toward a life that still has breath and, with it, a chance to respond.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the text does not name him. Here the author acknowledges that God is sovereign and that the judgment was no accident. So instead of blaming God, he calls the people to examine themselves and return to Him.

For today: when difficulty comes, before you complain, pause and pray honestly. Ask God whether there is something you need to correct. Even in pain, the life you have is an opportunity to return to Him and receive His mercy.
exp.4:14:
What it says: The people confess that there is no longer any joy in their hearts. That festive dance has turned into mourning, that is, into sorrow and grief over a great loss.

Context: Lamentations is a lament over the fall of Jerusalem, probably after the Babylonian invasion. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. Here the suffering community speaks: the young men labor as slaves, the elders no longer gather at the city gate, and the music has stopped. The verses that follow acknowledge that sin played a part in this tragedy.

For today: When pain comes, there is no need to pretend to be joyful. You can bring your sadness to God with honesty, as this people does. Lamenting before Him is a form of faith, because it trusts that God listens and can restore.
exp.2:54:
This verse says the person called on God by his name from a very deep and dark place. "To call upon" means to cry out or ask God for help. A "low dungeon" can also be understood as a deep pit or cell, a place with no way out. God appears as the only one to turn to when everything seems lost.

The speaker in Lamentations is usually taken to be a poet mourning the fall of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the book does not state this clearly. In chapter 3 he speaks in the first person, perhaps for himself and also for all his people. He describes anguish: stones piled on him, waters covering him, a sense of death. Even so, he prays, and God answers him: "Fear not."

For today: when you feel trapped or without strength, do not wait until you have beautiful words. Cry out to God sincerely, from wherever you are. He hears even the deepest cry.
exp.2:46:
The explanation says that the people lived in fear and fell into traps, like an animal caught. The word "snare" in the verse names a trap or net. "Desolation" means devastation, leaving the land laid waste. "Destruction" means ruin, something broken to pieces.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so openly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians, around 586 B.C. He speaks on behalf of the people, who feel humbled before the nations, and his grief is so great that he goes on with rivers of tears.

For today: when you go through loss or fear, do not pretend you are fine. This Scripture shows that weeping and telling God honestly what hurts is a form of faith. Tell God your pain today, in your own words.
exp.3:1:
This verse compares the people of Jerusalem to fine gold, something very precious. But now they are treated as ordinary clay jars, made by a potter, that is, common objects that are easily broken. The words "precious" and "valued" are rewritten here: the sons of Zion were once of great worth, and now they are treated as things of little worth.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem, probably before the Babylonian army, around 586 BC. He describes the pain of a people who lost their dignity, their temple, and even their security.

For today: our worth does not depend on how we are treated or on our falls. When someone feels despised, they can remember that God sees them with compassion. And if we know someone who is wounded, let us treat them with dignity and help them.
exp.2:65:
The explanation says the author asks God to pursue his enemies in his anger and destroy them, so that they no longer exist under the heavens. "Pursue them" means to chase after them without rest. "Anger" is very strong wrath. "Destroy" means to crush them or bring them to ruin. "Lord" is the name of God.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem, wounded by the mockery and cruelty of his enemies. It is a prayer of grief that leaves justice in God's hands rather than in one's own. Scholars understand these prayers in different ways.

For today: when someone has hurt you, you can be honest with God about your pain and your anger. Entrust justice to him rather than taking revenge. Jesus also taught us to pray for those who mistreat us (Matthew 5:44).
exp.3:4:
They that ate the finest foods are now left destitute and ruined in the streets. Those who were raised in clothing dyed scarlet, a very costly red dye used by the wealthy, now cling to dunghills, that is, to heaps of refuse, searching for anything to survive.

The one speaking is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. He mourns for Jerusalem after the siege and the fall of the city to Babylon, around 586 B.C. The hunger was so terrible that not even the rich were spared. The book presents this as a consequence of the people's sin.

Today, this verse reminds us that wealth and comfort are not a secure foundation. We can be thankful for what we have, live it with humility, and share it with those in need, without waiting for hard times to arrive.
exp.2:48:
It says the eyes of the one speaking "trickle," that is, pour out tears like drops that fall without stopping. They do not stop weeping because there is no relief, meaning no rest or comfort for his pain.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so explicitly. He weeps over the destruction of Jerusalem and the suffering of his people. The verses that follow show that his weeping continues until God looks down and sees from heaven. His grief is also a way of waiting on God.

For today: when pain does not leave quickly, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can weep honestly before God and keep hoping that He sees you. You can also patiently accompany someone who is suffering, without rushing them to feel better.
exp.0:6:
What it says: Jerusalem, when her people fell into the hands of the enemy and no one helped her, remembered the pain and the failures of her past, and also all the precious things she had possessed since long ago. Her enemies saw her and mocked her for her days of rest. The "pleasant things" are her treasures and blessings. To "mock" means to scorn someone with contempt. The "days of rest" were the days of rest and worship that God had given to Israel. Some scholars think the mocking was about her fall or her ending; the Hebrew text can be understood in several ways.

Context: Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem, probably in 586 B.C. by Babylon. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not state this clearly. Here the author describes the city as an abandoned woman who, in her loneliness, remembers what she has lost and acknowledges that her rebellions had consequences.

For today: When we go through difficult times, we can pause honestly, acknowledge our mistakes without sinking into guilt, and turn to God, who hears those who cry out to Him.
exp.1:4:
God acted against Israel as if he were an enemy. He allowed her palaces and her strongholds to fall, and so the grief grew among the people of Judah. "Daughter of Judah" is a poetic way of speaking about the people of Judah. "Swallowed up" means that he utterly destroyed or tore down. "Mourning and lamentation" means weeping and complaint over a great loss.

Lamentations is a song of sorrow over the fall of Jerusalem, which took place in 586 BC. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. The poet sees the destruction as the consequence of God's judgment for the sin of the people. He speaks with pain and with honesty.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand why, you can bring your pain before God without disguises. Lamenting before him is a form of faith, because you keep coming to him.
exp.4:13:
It says that the elders no longer sit at the city gate, and that the young men have stopped singing. The word "young men" here refers to the men who are young. In that time, the gate was the place where the elders gathered to give counsel, settle disputes, and look after the life of the people.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the text does not say so clearly. He mourns for Jerusalem after it was destroyed by the Babylonians. Without its leaders and its joy, the city fell into silence. The people acknowledge that they suffer because of their sin (v. 16).

For today: when sadness silences the music of your life, do not keep it quiet. Bring it before God with sincerity, as this book does. And value the elders who give counsel and the young people who bring joy.
exp.1:11:
Small children, hungry, were asking their mothers for bread and wine, but there was nothing left. They fainted in the streets like wounded soldiers, and at the end they died in their mothers' arms. The phrase about their lives being poured out is not explained further here, so the sense of their life slipping away little by little is simply carried in the verse itself.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. He mourns for Jerusalem after it was besieged and destroyed by Babylon. The hunger was terrible, and the writer laments that the false prophets did not speak the truth about the sin of the people.

Today we can learn not to ignore the pain of children who go hungry or lack what they need. God grieves with those who suffer, and invites us to weep with them and to help in concrete ways: sharing food, supporting a family, or serving at a community kitchen.
exp.0:3:
The ways that led to Jerusalem (Zion) are in mourning, because no one travels to the holy feasts anymore. The city's gates lie in ruins, her priests groan in grief, her young women suffer, and the whole city lives in bitterness.

The sentence about "solemn feasts" and "highways" can be rewritten as: The feasts are the festivals God commanded to be kept, and the ways are the roads. "Desolate" means ruined.

The book is a lament over the fall of Jerusalem, probably before Babylon, around 586 B.C. Tradition ascribes it to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. Here the poet speaks, describing the city as a wounded widow. The verses that follow explain that the people suffered because of their rebellions against God.

For today: when grief reaches you, do not hide it or pretend it away. This book teaches us to weep honestly before God. Bringing your sorrow to him in prayer is a step of faith, not of weakness.
exp.0:21:
It says that God should take into account all the wickedness of the enemies and deal with them as he dealt with the one speaking, because of his rebellions. The words "Let all their wickedness come before thee" mean "let it come before your presence." "Sighs" are groans of deep sorrow. The one speaking confesses that his heart is sick with sadness.

Jerusalem speaks here, pictured as an afflicted woman, at the end of the first lament. The city was destroyed and its people carried into exile. She acknowledges that her own rebellion against God brought the punishment, but she also sees that her neighbors mocked her fall. For this reason she asks for justice. It is an honest cry, and scholars understand it as prayer, not as personal revenge.

Today we can bring our pain to God with complete sincerity, acknowledging our failures without hiding them, and leave justice in his hands instead of taking it ourselves.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that God did what he had long before announced. He destroyed Jerusalem without showing pity, allowed its enemies to rejoice, and gave them strength over it. "He has set up the horn of thine adversaries" means that he gave them power and victory, because the horn was a symbol of strength.

Here speaks the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He mourns for Jerusalem after its fall before Babylon. He acknowledges that this was not chance: the people had been warned by their prophets that disobedience would bring judgment. The enemies mocked, but the grief sees it in the light of God's word.

For today: when you face the consequences of your mistakes, do not hide your pain or blame others. Be honest before God, acknowledge whatever is true, and cry out to him, because he is also the God who lets himself be reached by tears.
exp.4:10:
They abused the married women in Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and the young unmarried women in the towns of Judah. Here "ravished" means sexual abuse, and "maids" refers to young women who had not yet married. No one was spared, either in the main city or in the countryside.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the fall of Jerusalem, which is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. The speaker describes the suffering of the people after the Babylonian conquest: hunger, fear, and humiliation. The verse is part of a list of horrors that the people present before God.

For today: God is not shocked when we speak to him frankly about pain. We can pray with honesty, without embellishment. Moreover, this text calls us to defend and accompany those who suffer abuse, listening to them with respect and without judgment.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that Judah left her land because of suffering and harsh slavery. She lived among other nations and found no rest. Her pursuers caught up with her in narrow places, with no way out and no escape. The word "fled" in this verse means "went away."

Here the author of Lamentations speaks. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the book does not state this clearly. He mourns for Jerusalem after its destruction by Babylon in 586 BC. The verses that follow explain that God allowed this affliction because of the people's many rebellions.

For today: when you go through times of anguish, do not face them in silence or alone. This book shows us that one can grieve honestly before God. Tell him your pain, acknowledge whatever you need to correct, and seek the support of other believers.
exp.2:64:
The explanation says that the author asks God to leave his enemies with "sorrow of heart," an old-fashioned expression that can be understood as hardness, blindness, or anguish of the heart. Then it adds "thy curse unto them," meaning that God's curse should fall on them. Some translations read this as a veil or pain in the heart; the Hebrew is difficult and is interpreted in several ways.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. He is suffering mockery and persecution, and "their song" refers to the theme of their mockery. After the fall of Jerusalem, he cries out to God to do justice and not to take vengeance himself.

For today: when you are wounded unjustly, you can bring your pain and your anger honestly to God, leaving justice in his hands. Jesus, moreover, teaches us to pray for those who harm us.
exp.3:6:
This verse describes the "Nazarites" of Jerusalem as people whose skin was white as snow, bright as milk, with a healthy color like rubies, and a beauty like sapphire. Here "Nazarites" probably refers to people who were set apart or consecrated, though some think it speaks of princes or nobles. "Her Nazarites" here likely refers to the form or bearing of their bodies, meaning their appearance or figure.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem and recalls how the best of the people once were, to show the contrast with the hunger and ruin that came afterward, as the following verses say.

For today: health, reputation, or position can change suddenly. Let us not place our security in what can be lost, but in God, who remains faithful even in times of sorrow.
exp.0:1:
It says that Jerusalem, pictured as a woman, weeps bitterly through the night, and her tears run down her face. No one comforts her. The "lovers" are the allies and nations that once seemed to support her. The phrase about her friends means they betrayed her and even became her enemies.

The book of Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so. The speaker is the poet, who describes the city as a helpless widow. The grief is deep because the allies she trusted did not help her.

Today it reminds us that God is not alarmed by our tears, and that the Bible makes room for sincere weeping. If someone failed you in your pain, do not keep it silent: bring it to God in prayer and seek faithful people who will walk alongside you.
exp.2:55:
Here the speaker remembers that God already heard him when he cried out from a very dark place. Now he asks God not to hide His ear, that is, not to pretend He is deaf. The phrase "at my breathing" means at my relief, at my being able to breathe again. Some versions translate it differently, as "my relief" and "my cry," and not all scholars agree on how those words relate to one another.

The speaker is the poet of Lamentations, who suffers in the midst of Jerusalem's ruin. He speaks in the first person, perhaps for himself or on behalf of his people; this is debated. His words come from an anguish so great that he feels drowned by waters and shut in a deep prison, yet he remembers that God has answered before.

For today: when you are overwhelmed, remember how God helped you before, and pray with that confidence. Ask Him for relief sincerely, without pretending to a strength you do not have.
exp.2:61:
This verse says that enemies speak against the one who is suffering, and that their schemes against him do not stop all day long. "The lips" are their words, what they whisper and say. "Rose up" means they set themselves in opposition. "Device" means a plan or intention.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. In chapter 3 he speaks of his personal pain, and at the same time he seems to voice the grief of his people after the fall of Jerusalem. Here he tells God how his adversaries attack him with mockery and plots. The neighboring verses show that he trusts God sees everything and will do justice.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you or makes you feel persecuted, do not carry that distress alone. Tell God honestly what you hear and feel, and leave justice in his hands, without taking revenge.
exp.0:9:
The explanation says that the enemy stretched out his hand to take all the treasures of Jerusalem. Furthermore, the city saw with grief that foreign people were entering the sanctuary, the temple. God had commanded that those nations should not enter his congregation, that is, the assembly of God's people. "Pleasant things" are valuable objects, probably those of the temple and the city.

The poet of Lamentations speaks, weeping for Jerusalem, and in other verses the city itself speaks. It is a song of mourning over the destruction of the city by Babylon, in 586 B.C. The text says it happened because of the people's sin. Even so, the writer does not stay silent: he cries out to God and asks him to look upon their affliction.

For today: when you suffer because of your mistakes or because of things you have lost, do not hide from God. You can bring him your pain honestly, acknowledge what you did wrong, and ask him to look upon you with compassion.
exp.2:42:
It says God showed his anger with force. "You have covered yourself with anger" is like spreading a net or a curtain: his anger fell on the people. "You pursued us" speaks of a discipline they felt was unstoppable. "You slew, you have not pitied" describes the harshness of the punishment, with no visible relief.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem. In the verses before, the people acknowledge their rebellion. Now he describes with pain what they lived through as God's judgment. It is an honest prayer, made out of suffering.

For today: when you go through pain or the consequences of your mistakes, you can speak to God with sincerity, without pretending. Acknowledge your fault, express your pain, and keep drawing near to Him. Later in this same book, it speaks of his mercy being renewed every morning.
exp.3:13:
They wandered aimlessly through the streets, like blind people who stumble along. They were stained with blood, so filthy that no one wanted to touch their clothes. The phrase about stumbling means they staggered and wavered, and the word for stained means they were marked and made impure.

The one speaking is the poet of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. He blames above all the religious leaders, who were meant to guide the people but tolerated injustice and violence. The blood speaks of moral guilt, and the blindness speaks of having lost the guidance of God.

For today: those who lead others, in the church, in the family, or at work, carry a great responsibility. Let us ask God for integrity, and let us not forget to pray for our leaders. If we have failed, let us seek his forgiveness and his light.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that the speaker's soul cannot forget his suffering. The soul "hath them still in remembrance," which means it keeps coming back to those memories again and again. To be "humbled in me" here means to be brought low, sunk down by sorrow. Some modern translations put it as "my soul is downcast within me."

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem. At the darkest point of his complaint, he admits that he has almost lost hope. But the next verse brings a turn: as he remembers God's mercy, hope returns.

For today: you do not have to pretend that pain does not exist. You can tell God honestly how you feel. And when sad memories surround you, try to remember something of God's faithfulness in your own life as well. In this way, your hope can rise little by little.
exp.4:7:
The explanation says that people who used to be of a lower class, such as servants or slaves, now rule over God's people. The phrase "have ruled over us" means they dominated and governed with power. And no one could rescue them from their hands.

The speaker is the people of Judah, who mourn after the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon. The servants may be officials of the conquerors, or people of little authority who now govern. Scholars understand this in several ways. The people recognize that they suffer because of their own sins and the sins of their ancestors, and they feel they have no help.

For today: when you feel trapped or without a way out, be honest with God in prayer, as this people was. Do not hide your pain. Lamentations teaches that one can grieve and still turn back to God, waiting for his mercy.

sum.2: In this chapter, the author describes his pain and suffering with grief, as if God himself had surrounded him and wounded him. But in the middle of his distress, he remembers that God's mercy and faithfulness are new every morning, and so he decides to wait for Him. He invites the people to turn back to God, and at the end he cries out for help and justice.
sum.1: Lamentations 2 describes, with deep grief, how God, in his anger, allowed Jerusalem to be destroyed. Its walls, its temple, and its leaders all fell, and the false prophets did not warn the city of its sin. The author mourns the hunger of the children and calls the people to cry out to God. The chapter ends with an anguished prayer asking God to look upon their suffering.
sum.4: In this chapter the people ask God to remember their shame and suffering. They have lost their homes, they go hungry, and they live under oppression. They acknowledge that they have sinned and that they are suffering because of it. Even so, they trust that God reigns forever, and they ask him to bring them back to himself and renew their days.
sum.0: Jerusalem, once great and full of people, is left alone and weeping, like a widow, after being defeated and taken into captivity. The text acknowledges that this came because of her sins and that God is just, yet the people suffer without comfort and ask God to look at their pain. They also pray that their enemies will receive punishment.
sum.3: Lamentations 4 describes with grief the fall of Jerusalem: the famine, the ruin, and the shame of the people, whose sins, especially those of prophets and priests, brought God's judgment. In the end, the punishment of Zion comes to an end, but Edom will be judged.
